Hackers have targeted blood plasma storage facilities in France and supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe, raising concerns about cybersecurity and public safety.


## Hackers Target Blood Storage Facilities and Supermarket Refrigeration Systems Across Europe


A major cybersecurity incident targeting refrigeration systems across Europe has raised serious concerns about the security of essential services, including healthcare and food supply networks. Hackers reportedly manipulated temperature settings in blood plasma storage facilities in France, while supermarket refrigerators and freezers were also affected in several European countries.


The attacks, reported on 2 November 2026, highlight the growing risks associated with connected technology and the potential consequences of cybercriminals gaining access to systems responsible for protecting essential supplies.


According to the French Blood Establishment (EFS), three of its cold-storage facilities were affected by the incident. Although the attackers reportedly attempted to increase refrigeration temperatures to dangerously high levels, monitoring systems detected the unusual activity before any blood samples were damaged.


The incident is now being investigated by French authorities, while cybersecurity officials across Europe are assessing the wider implications.


## Blood Plasma Refrigerators Targeted in France


The cyberattack against France's blood storage infrastructure has attracted particular attention because of the potential risks to healthcare services.


Blood plasma and other blood products require carefully controlled storage conditions to maintain their quality and safety. Any unauthorised changes to refrigeration settings could potentially compromise valuable medical supplies.


The French Blood Establishment confirmed that three of its cold-storage locations experienced a cyber incident involving their refrigeration control systems.


In its statement, the organisation explained that temperature settings and defrosting thresholds had been increased to extremely high levels. However, it did not publicly confirm the exact temperatures recorded during the incident.


French investigative publication *Le Canard Enchaîné* , which first reported the attack, claimed that the refrigeration systems had been reprogrammed from minus 30 degrees Celsius to 110 degrees Celsius.


Despite the alarming reported temperature changes, the organisation's monitoring systems identified the problem before any stored samples suffered damage.


The incident demonstrates how cyberattacks targeting operational technology can create serious risks even when attackers do not directly access medical records or other confidential information.


## Supermarket Fridges and Freezers Also Hit by Cyberattacks


The attack on French blood storage facilities occurred on the same day that supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe reportedly experienced similar cyber incidents.


According to reports, supermarket chains in at least 10 countries were affected, with hackers targeting connected refrigerators and freezers.


A limited number of supermarket freezers in the United Kingdom were also impacted, according to Dr Richard Horne, head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC).


Although the full extent of the disruption remains unclear, the incidents have raised questions about the vulnerability of refrigeration equipment connected to modern digital networks.


Supermarkets depend on refrigeration systems to preserve perishable products, including meat, dairy products, seafood and frozen foods. If temperature controls are compromised, businesses could face significant financial losses, food safety concerns and supply chain disruption.


Authorities have not confirmed whether the attacks on supermarket equipment and French blood storage facilities were coordinated or carried out by the same individuals.


Furthermore, no hacking group or cybercriminal organisation has publicly claimed responsibility for the incidents.


## European Authorities Investigate the Growing Cybersecurity Threat


The incidents have prompted discussions among European officials about improving cooperation and strengthening protection for critical infrastructure.


European Union spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed that discussions were taking place with national authorities to coordinate an appropriate response.


He stressed the importance of collective preparedness and resilience when dealing with cyber incidents affecting essential services.


The concern is not limited to refrigeration equipment. Healthcare facilities, energy providers, water networks, transport systems and food distribution companies increasingly depend on interconnected digital infrastructure.


A successful cyberattack against these systems could potentially disrupt services that millions of people rely on every day.


The latest incidents demonstrate why cybersecurity must be treated as a public safety priority rather than simply an information technology issue.


## NCSC Warns Organisations About Outdated Technology


The UK's National Cyber Security Centre has also warned that many organisations have failed to invest sufficiently in updating and securing their technology infrastructure.


Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, NCSC chief Dr Richard Horne highlighted the vulnerabilities created by outdated computer systems.


He warned that artificial intelligence is making it easier for hostile actors to identify weaknesses and exploit them.


According to Horne, organisations across society continue to rely on technology that has not received the necessary investment to remain secure against increasingly sophisticated threats.


His comments reflect wider concerns among cybersecurity professionals that older operational technology systems may be particularly vulnerable.


Many refrigeration systems, industrial controllers and building management platforms were originally designed to maintain operational efficiency rather than defend against modern cyberattacks.


When these systems are connected to corporate networks or the internet without appropriate security protections, they can become attractive targets for cybercriminals.


## Artificial Intelligence Could Make Cyberattacks More Dangerous


Artificial intelligence is becoming an increasingly important factor in the global cybersecurity landscape.


While AI offers significant benefits for businesses, healthcare organisations and public services, it can also be misused by malicious actors.


Cybercriminals may use AI-powered tools to identify system weaknesses, automate reconnaissance and increase the speed at which attacks are developed and executed.


This creates additional challenges for organisations that lack experienced cybersecurity teams or adequate security investment.


Barry Mainz, chief executive of cybersecurity company Forescout, warned that cyberattacks are no longer exclusively focused on stealing information.


He explained that gaining access to systems controlling hospitals, water supplies, energy networks, transport infrastructure and food distribution can create risks for public health, national security and public safety.


His warning highlights an important shift in the nature of modern cybercrime. Instead of targeting only personal information or financial records, attackers may increasingly focus on the digital systems that operate essential services.


## Why Critical Infrastructure Needs Stronger Cybersecurity


The refrigeration attacks underline the importance of protecting operational technology, commonly known as OT.


Operational technology includes the hardware and software responsible for monitoring and controlling physical equipment, including industrial machinery, temperature sensors, refrigeration units and manufacturing systems.


Unlike conventional office computers, these systems can directly influence physical environments.


For example, unauthorised access to a refrigeration controller could allow an attacker to manipulate temperature settings, interfere with alarms or disrupt normal equipment operations.


Organisations responsible for essential services should therefore consider several important security measures:


- **Regular software updates:** Outdated systems should be identified and updated wherever possible to reduce known vulnerabilities.
- **Network segmentation:** Critical operational equipment should be separated from less sensitive corporate networks.
- **Continuous monitoring:** Organisations should monitor unusual system activity and unexpected changes to operational settings.
- **Access controls:** Strong authentication and restricted permissions can help prevent unauthorised access.
- **Incident response planning:** Businesses should have procedures for identifying, containing and recovering from cyberattacks.
- **Staff training:** Employees should understand cybersecurity risks and know how to report suspicious activity.


These measures can help reduce the likelihood of successful attacks and limit their consequences when security breaches occur.


## What the Latest Attacks Mean for European Businesses


The incidents affecting blood storage facilities and supermarket refrigeration systems provide a warning to businesses operating essential infrastructure.


Digital transformation has improved efficiency across many industries, but greater connectivity also introduces additional security challenges.


Companies can no longer assume that equipment designed for physical operations is protected simply because it is not a traditional computer system.


Refrigeration networks, industrial control systems and automated monitoring equipment all require appropriate cybersecurity protections.


For healthcare providers, the consequences of a compromised system could extend beyond financial losses. Any disruption involving medical supplies could potentially affect patient care.


For supermarkets, refrigeration failures could result in wasted products, operational disruption and increased costs.


As cyber threats continue to evolve, organisations must invest in modern security systems, employee awareness and effective emergency response strategies.


## Conclusion


The cyberattacks targeting blood plasma refrigeration facilities in France and supermarket freezers across Europe have highlighted the growing vulnerability of essential infrastructure.


Although monitoring systems reportedly prevented damage to stored blood products, the incident demonstrates how digital attacks can threaten physical equipment and services that people depend on.


With artificial intelligence potentially increasing the speed and scale of cybercrime, governments and businesses must take a more proactive approach to protecting critical systems.


The priority now is to strengthen cybersecurity, modernise outdated technology and ensure that essential services remain protected against increasingly sophisticated digital threats.
